claims.text: High-temperature oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by the formation kinetics of a continuous, adherent, passivating oxide scale.
Protective oxide scales in these alloys are enriched in passivating alloying elements such as Cr or Al.
Increasing the concentration of Cr or Al accelerates formation of a protective oxide barrier.
The protective oxide barrier limits further oxidation.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuous, thin, adherent surface oxide scale.
The oxide scale forms through diffusion of passivating elements from the alloy bulk to the surface, followed by their oxidation.
Greater availability of passivating elements increases early nucleation and growth of the protective oxide layer.
Oxide-scale formation in the proposed regime is diffusion controlled.
The protective scale acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress and thereby slows oxidation kinetics.
Slower oxidation kinetics preserve material integrity during cyclic high-temperature exposure.
Alloys with increased passivating-element concentrations will form more uniform and adherent oxide scales than the baseline alloy.
Alloys with increased passivating-element concentrations will exhibit lower oxidation-induced mass gain than the baseline alloy.
Alloys with increased passivating-element concentrations will show less oxide spallation and cracking than the baseline alloy.
Under identical high-temperature exposure, the baseline alloy develops a less protective scale, greater mass gain, and more degradation than the composition enriched in passivating elements.
The proposed diffusion-controlled protective mechanism applies approximately from 700°C to 1200°C.
At substantially higher temperatures or in environments containing additional corrosive species, other degradation mechanisms may supersede protective oxide formation.
